newsitem.title: THAILAND: Cambodia's Ranariddh can't expect war aid-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Ranariddh can't expect war aid-analysts.

text.p: Cambodia's Prince Norodom Ranariddh has little chance of securing the support necessary to fight his way back into power after being ousted as prime minister in a bloody coup last weekend, military analysts say.
Ranariddh called for talks after his forces were defeated in two days of fighting in Phnom Penh by soldiers of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, now Cambodia's de facto ruler.
At the same time he warned of a return to civil war, but this was something he was ill-equipped to fight, the Bangkok-based analysts said.
In the 1980s it was a different story.

Then Ranariddh's faction was part of a guerrilla alliance backed staunchly by the West with arms and money against Hun Sen, a man first put into power by communist Vietnam and backed by the then Soviet bloc.

"The big difference between now and the 1980s is that the international context has changed," said a foreign military attache. "The Cold War is not here any more and it doesn't make sense to use Cambodia to fight proxy battles any more."

In the 1980s, Ranariddh's men and the other guerrilla factions relied on Thai support in fighting their war. Thailand was a logistical gateway for arms and supplies and a fallback position for the guerrillas when the going got tough.
Now Bangkok's policy is far less favourable to the prince. No longer feeling threatened by Vietnam, Bangkok appears willing to work with the government of the day in Phnom Penh.
This week, powerful Thai army commander in chief General Chetta Thanajaro said he did not believe any foreign country would provide military support to a Cambodian faction.
"Without support from outside the country the fighting will not last long and they will eventually reconcile."

On Wednesday, Cambodia's U.N. ambassador Prince Sisowath Sirirath said Ranariddh's followers would mass troops in the second city, western Battambang, and establish a base for resistance. But he added that talks were preferable to war.
Sisowath said royalist forces had disarmed more than 2,000 opposing soldiers. There has been no independent confirmation.

Robert Karniol, Asia-Pacific editor of the defence magazine Jane's Defence Weekly, said that without foreign aid, especially from Thailand, Ranariddh's forces would not be able to achieve much, even with the help of hardline Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
"They have the capability to fight for a time -- for how long, nobody really knows," Karniol said. "But it's unlikely they will be able to do anything much substantial or sustained.

"Much depends on what kind of weapons stockpiles they have. It would be difficult for them to get new weapons. What they would be able to get would be drips and drabs -- stuff bought on the black market and smuggled in."

The military attache estimated the strength of Ranariddh's forces and the hardline Khmer Rouge at only a few thousand fighters. A breakaway Khmer Rouge faction on the western border with Thailand has said it will remain neutral in any fighting.
The attache estimated Hun Sen had up to about 90,000 troops but probably a much lower frontline fighting strength.

The strength of Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party and the Khmer Rouge is in the landlocked north and northwest and weapons and other supplies would have to pass through foreign or government territory to reach them.

"FUNCINPEC are in a tough position. To do anything significant militarily they need substantial logistics. They can't get that without a favourable international environment and it doesn't appear they'll get that," the attache said.

Should Ranariddh's forces opt to try to fight alongside the Khmer Rouge -- international pariahs after their rule in the 1970s which killed more than a million Cambodians -- what the prince might gain militarily he would lose politically as a result of the association, Karniol said.
"One alternative," said Karniol, "would be for them to try to hold out in the bush and wait for some kind of implosion in Phnom Penh. But that doesn't look too likely at the moment."
Nor do the talks Ranariddh has urged appear likely.
"It's too late and it is not necessary. Everything is over," Hun Sen said on Sunday night in response to a reconciliation appeal made by Ranariddh's father, King Norodom Sihanouk.
